Most business plans fail before they're finished, because nobody did the research first.

I've watched it happen from every side of the table. I've been the salesman on the floor, the contractor on the job site, the veteran who learned that the plan only works if the recon was right, and the owner building multiple businesses at once.

The pattern is always the same. People skip the research, guess at the market, and build the plan on assumptions. Then they wonder why the numbers don't hold.

Here's what I do instead, and what I'm now taking on as contract work:

🔎 Market research and competitive analysis
Who's actually buying, who you're up against, and where the gap is.

📊 Business plans built on real numbers
Lean roadmaps for founders, and full lender or investor-ready plans with projections.

🚀 Business development and go-to-market strategy
New products, new channels, new markets, and a plan to get there.

⚙️ Operations analysis
Finding the bottlenecks that cost you money, and fixing them with smart systems and AI where it makes sense.

Recent work has included full proposal packages for local businesses, a complete bid package for a federal service solicitation, and ongoing local market intelligence for business owners in the Tulsa area.

If you're a founder, a small business owner, or a team that needs research and strategy done right without hiring full-time, send me a message. I scope every project before I quote it, so you pay for what you actually need.

If you want to go GOD-level with API design,
learn these 7 protocols (save now):


1 REST (Representational State Transfer)
↳ Uses resources & standard HTTP methods via a stateless interface
↳ Use cases: CRUD APIs for web & mobile apps

===

2 GraphQL
↳ Lets clients request exactly the data they need
↳ Use cases: apps with complex and/or changing data requirements

===

3 WebSockets
↳ Keeps a bidirectional connection open between client & server
↳ Use cases: chat, multiplayer games & real-time updates

===

4 gRPC (Google Remote Procedure Call)
↳ Calls remote services via strongly typed contracts
↳ Use cases: fast communication between internal microservices

===

5 Webhooks
↳ Sends event notifications from one system to another
↳ Use cases: real-time AI agents & event-driven workflows

===

6 MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport)
↳ Sends lightweight messages using publish-subscribe messaging
↳ Use cases: IoT devices & unreliable or low-bandwidth networks

===

7 SSE (Server-Sent Events)
↳ Streams updates from a server to a client over HTTP
↳ Use cases: live feeds, notifications & AI response streaming

Anything else you'd add?

===

👋 PS - Want to make your AI agents real-time?

Polling for updates adds unnecessary latency to agent workflows.

Webhooks let your agents react to events as they happen. But running reliable webhook infrastructure means dealing with failed endpoints, retries, security & monitoring.

Svix handles that infrastructure for you, including automatic retries, signing, observability & idempotency support.

🚀 Recruitment is changing. But great recruitment is still about people.
AI can source candidates.
AI can screen CVs.
AI can help identify skills.
But it can't replace a trusted relationship.
And I think that's becoming more important, not less.
In 2026, recruitment is moving towards skills over titles, quality over quantity and technology-supported hiring. At the same time, human connections are becoming increasingly valuable as applications become easier to generate — and harder to differentiate. 
So, what do I do differently?
🤝 I build relationships before there is a vacancy.
I want to understand professionals before I'm trying to place them — and understand my clients before they urgently need someone.
🎯 I look beyond the CV.
What can you actually do? What motivates you? What environment helps you perform? Where do you want your career to go?
💬 I have real conversations.
AI is a fantastic tool, but recruitment decisions affect careers, teams and businesses. That requires listening, challenging and sometimes giving advice people don't necessarily expect.
📊 I bring market knowledge to both sides.
For candidates: career direction, salary expectations, CV and interview support.
For clients: talent availability, realistic expectations, salary benchmarking, Permanent vs Contract/Freelance options and what I'm hearing directly from the market.
❤️ And I stay involved.
From the first conversation to shortlist, interview, feedback, negotiation and beyond.
Not every candidate I speak to will be right for every client.
Not every opportunity will be right for every professional.
And that's exactly the point.
My job isn't to create the most matches.
It's to create the right ones.
So whether you're a Technology professional evaluating your next chapter, a freelancer considering your next project, or a business thinking about the talent you'll need next:
☕ Let's have a conversation before it becomes urgent.

Three architectures. One request. Watch where they end up.

Every one of them finishes in the same place, which is the part people skip
past when they argue about this.

The response comes back either way. What changes is everything in between,
and what that costs you.

𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗵

One deployable unit. One process. Scale it by running more copies of the whole
thing.

Testing is honest here. One environment, one end-to-end suite. Slow, but you can
actually trust a green run.

𝗠𝗶𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀

Many deployable units. Calls that cross a service boundary go over the network,
which means they can be slow, and they can fail.

Testing changes completely. Without contract tests you are not testing, you are
hoping. Your hardest problem stops being the tests and becomes the environment.

𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀

No servers to manage. You still ship an artifact, it just runs somewhere you
do not operate.

On Lambda you get 900 seconds of execution and a default concurrency of 1,000
per region, and that default is raisable.

Testing gets a new failure mode. Cold starts look exactly like flaky tests until
you measure them separately.

None of these is the right answer. They are three different bills for the same
outcome.

Which one are you on, and would you pick it again?

Hollywood’s unions are forcing a part of the AI debate into territory that is far less speculative than the question of what artificial intelligence might eventually become.

In June, SAG-AFTRA members ratified their new TV/Theatrical agreement with 91.42% approval. Among its provisions are stronger restrictions on synthetic performers and additional protections around digital replicas.

Producers wishing to use a synthetic in a human role must notify the union and bargain over its use, while the agreement establishes a principle favouring human performance. The WGA’s 2026 agreement moves into another part of the value chain: companies must now notify the Guild when writers’ work is licensed to train a commercial generative-AI system. 

These developments interest me because Hollywood is effectively asking a different AI-risk question. Much of the technology debate concentrates on the capabilities machines may acquire: autonomy, increasingly sophisticated reasoning and, at the extreme, whether future systems could become difficult for humans to control.

Creative workers are confronting the inverse question: as machines acquire more capabilities, what do humans retain control over?

Consider an actor’s face or voice. Historically, accessing the economic value of a performance generally required hiring the performer. Digital replication begins to separate the two. A person can perform once, while a technological representation of elements of that performance may potentially be reused elsewhere.

The economic asset is therefore no longer only labour. It can also become the reproducible digital representation of labour.

That changes the bargaining problem profoundly. Compensation is one issue, but so are consent, duration of use, ownership, reuse and the circumstances under which a synthetic alternative can substitute for another human engagement. SAG-AFTRA itself frames its AI guardrails around consent, compensation and control.
 
Writing introduces a related complication. Once existing creative work can contribute to systems capable of producing new outputs, the boundary between creation and productive input becomes harder to ignore. The WGA’s notification provision is significant precisely because it begins bringing the licensing of that input into the contractual relationship.
 
This is why I would not separate today’s labour disputes from the larger AI-risk conversation. They operate on different timescales, but they concern the same underlying allocation of power: what machines are permitted to do, what humans continue to control, and which institutions define the boundary between the two.

Long before we know whether humanity can retain control over the most advanced AI systems, contracts such as these are already determining something much more immediate:

- How much control humans retain over the economic value of their own identity and creative work.

I left the East Bay Founders Customer Success in the AI Era event still thinking about one question: How do you scale trust?

Nathan Trueblood said trust comes from following through, delivering value, and building a real relationship. That never changes. What changes is how you scale it, from one person to systems, structure, and a culture where everyone owns the customer.

Kimthu Doan talked about hiring for that shift. At an early stage, the right fit is customer obsession, not a polished resume.

The line that hit hardest was about the AI era. Customers are not signing longer contracts anymore. The moment a deal closes, you have to think about renewal, anchoring every conversation around the outcomes the customer needs.

The one piece I am carrying forward is: Activity is not value. More tickets does not mean better, and silence is bad, but noise is not the goal either. That balance from all the signals in true unison is a fine-tuned dance that can be achieved when an entire organization owns the customer and the process to success and value. 

Grateful for rooms like this and for founders willing to share what they are actually wrestling with.

Thanks to Matthew Herrick and Herrick Wealth Advisory for sponsoring the event, to Sugata Sanyal for putting together such insightful conversations, and to my friend Swapnil Amin for joining!

That’s an acceleration from the 34% growth reported in Q1. 

For a company already generating billions in annual revenue, maintaining mid-30% growth is significant.

2. AI is creating a new growth opportunity

Cloudflare is positioning itself as infrastructure for the “agentic Internet.”

AI agents need somewhere to run code, access APIs, interact with websites and securely communicate with other systems.

That plays directly into Cloudflare’s network + Workers + Security platform.

Cloudflare has also partnered with Anthropic to provide infrastructure for Claude-managed agents.

3. Cloudflare is becoming much more than a CDN

This is probably the most important part of the story.

Cloudflare started with its global network and CDN.

Today, it increasingly sells:

→ Cybersecurity
→ Zero Trust
→ DDoS & bot protection
→ Developer infrastructure
→ Serverless compute through Workers
→ AI infrastructure
→ Networking
→ Application security

The more products a customer uses, the more Cloudflare becomes embedded in their infrastructure.

4. Enterprise demand is getting stronger

Cloudflare said Q2 produced record growth in large customers and developers, while Current RPO grew 35% YoY.

It also closed its largest annual contract value deal ever in Q4 2025, worth an average $42.5 million per year. 

That suggests the opportunity isn’t limited to smaller internet companies anymore.

5. The company is aggressively building for AI

Cloudflare has been acquiring and hiring around the AI developer ecosystem.

It acquired VoidZero, bringing Vite and other JavaScript tooling into its platform, aiming to make deployment from local development to Cloudflare’s global network much easier. 

It has also been investing in AI infrastructure and inference efficiency. 

So investors aren’t just valuing Cloudflare for what it is today.

They’re increasingly valuing it for what it could become if AI agents become a major layer of Internet traffic.

And that is why the move from $218 → $359 is more interesting than the chart alone suggests.

The big question now:
Can Cloudflare turn the AI boom into another major growth engine without losing its current growth rate?

Your AI is making decisions faster than your governance can review them. That gap is now the single largest liability on your balance sheet that no one has priced in.

AI TRiSM (Trust, Risk, and Security Management) is emerging as the operating discipline that separates enterprises scaling AI safely from those accumulating invisible exposure. This is not a compliance checkbox. It is becoming a board-level capital allocation decision, on par with cybersecurity investment a decade ago.

Three implications every CXO should internalize. First, model opacity is now a shareholder risk. When AI systems influence pricing, credit, hiring, or clinical decisions, the inability to explain "why" is no longer a technical footnote, it is regulatory and reputational exposure that materializes in earnings calls, not IT tickets. Second, governance built after deployment is governance that arrives too late. Leading enterprises are embedding trust and risk controls into the model lifecycle itself, treating monitoring, drift detection, and bias auditing as continuous infrastructure, not periodic audits. Third, TRiSM is becoming a competitive differentiator, not just a defensive posture. Enterprises that can demonstrate verifiable AI trust will win regulated industries, enterprise contracts, and customer confidence faster than competitors still explaining their models after the fact.

The hidden trade-off leadership must confront: over-indexing on control can throttle innovation velocity, while under-investing invites systemic failure at scale. The winning posture is not maximum caution, it is engineered trust, calibrated governance that moves at the speed of deployment, not behind it.

The organizations treating AI TRiSM as a strategic capability, not a defensive cost center, will be the ones regulators trust, customers choose, and boards stop losing sleep over.

Where does your AI governance sit today, ahead of deployment, or cleaning up after it?

Spent tonight at East Bay Founders in San Ramon. Customer Success in the AI Era. Bishop Ranch.

East Bay Founders put operators in a room. Sugata Sanyal  hosted. Ted Hulsy and Emily Valencia helped build it. Matthew Herrick sponsored it.

Melissa McMillan showed an agentic dashboard running live. Usage, friction, risk, and what needs a human next. See the book in real time instead of waiting for the QBR.

Then someone asked the simple question. Who owns the customer.

Maranda Dziekonski did not give it to CS or sales. Everyone owns the customer.

Nathan Trueblood took that into the second panel. Trust still comes from follow through, real value, and a real relationship. What changes is how you scale it. From one person, to a system, to a culture.

Kimthu Doan on hiring. Early on, customer obsession beats a polished resume.

The line I am carrying home. Customers are not signing long contracts anymore. The day the deal closes, renewal is already the job.

Activity is not value. More tickets is not better. Silence is bad. Noise is not the goal. What is the customer doing that represents value to them.

Build the agents. Then spend the time you get back on the call that actually changes the account. The one where a person stays because another person showed up.

🤖 Single-Agent AI Assistants Are Being Replaced by Orchestrated Agent Networks
Across the industry in 2026, a quiet transition is accelerating: single-agent assistance is giving way to specialized agent chains. What's emerging is simultaneously more powerful and more complex: multiple agents orchestrating work across domains with minimal human re-prompting required.
🔴 THE CURRENT PATTERN
Most organizations deploy single AI assistants in isolation. One handles customer support. Another does code review. A third generates documentation. Each is specialized but disconnected. Humans become the orchestrators: prompting each tool, moving outputs between systems, making editorial calls, fixing handoff gaps. Productivity gains emerge. Efficiency lags.
🟡 THE EMERGING ALTERNATIVE BEING IMPLEMENTED
When one agent researches competitive positioning in parallel with another drafting narrative while a third flags regulatory risks and a fourth validates claims, work passes automatically between agents without human re-prompting or intervention. Results loop back for refinement or move forward to final output. The system coordinates itself with minimal human overhead.
🟠 THE DISCIPLINE REQUIRED
This architecture demands rigor: clear agent responsibilities, structured output contracts, async coordination, fallback logic when agents diverge, access governance. It's not complex for complexity's sake. It's rigorous structure enabling scale.
🟢 THE ORGANIZATIONAL SHIFT THAT EMERGES
Organizations operationalizing agent orchestration aren't hiring more prompt engineers. They're recruiting system architects who understand workflow design and reliability. Orchestration isn't about writing better prompts—it's about defining how specialized agents collaborate reliably. Roles shift: Product managers transition to workflow architects. QE teams test agent handoff reliability and failure scenarios.
🧮 THE ECONOMICS OF ORCHESTRATION
A human coordinating three tools spends roughly 40% of available time on coordination. Three agents coordinating themselves spend approximately 5% on coordination. That 35% efficiency delta compounds across projects. It explains why agent orchestration is becoming foundational for product velocity.

17 AI System Concepts Every Founder Should Understand Before Hiring an AI Agency

A founder once sent me an agency proposal that used 16 of these 17 terms. It did not contain a single number. The 1 term it skipped was evaluations.

Founders read charts like this as a shopping list. I read them as a bill of materials. Every box is something you pay for, maintain, and get blamed for when it breaks in front of a customer. Here is how I break it down.

4 of these boxes decide whether you have a product. Embeddings, vector databases, RAG, and context engineering. This is the part everyone demos. Getting it 80% right takes a week. The last 15% takes months, and that 15% is where your customer decides whether to trust it.

3 of them decide whether you have a business. Semantic caching, model routing, and an AI gateway. None of them show up in a demo, and together they set your gross margin. I once audited a product that lost money on every paying user because every question, including "what are your opening hours," went to the largest model available. Routing and caching fixed it in 2 weeks and cut inference spend by more than half.

5 of them decide how much risk you carry. Function calling, tool use, MCP, external integrations, and the agent harness. This is where AI starts writing to your CRM, sending emails, touching money. Every capability you hand an agent is a liability until you can prove how it behaves. My month 1 default: the agent drafts, a person approves.

3 of them decide whether it still works in month 6. The execution loop, memory, and guardrails. Most agent failures I get called in to fix live here. A loop that never terminates. Memory that leaks 1 customer's context into another's session. Guardrails added after a bad answer reached a client.

And 2 of them decide whether the other 15 are real. Observability and evaluations. If an agency cannot show you a test set, a baseline score, and a trace of every request in the first 2 weeks, you have no way to know what you are paying for.

So the most useful question to ask any agency is which of the 17 they would leave out, and why. Most products I scope need 8 to 10. Some need a classifier and a well-written SQL query, and I tell founders that on the first call, even when it shrinks my contract.

That is also why clients stay with me for years. From week 1, they own the evaluation set, the dashboards, and the cost per query. After that, every decision is based on numbers they can see, so the work shifts from building the system to growing it.

AGENTIC AI DEBATE: MCP vs Function Calling — are we solving the same problem twice?
Before MCP became one of the hottest terms in AI, developers were already connecting LLMs to external systems using:
Function Calling → APIs → Tools → Databases → Enterprise Applications
Now Model Context Protocol (MCP) introduces a standardized approach for exposing tools, resources, and context to AI applications.
So here's the question:
👉 When do you actually NEED MCP instead of regular function/tool calling?
🔧 FUNCTION / TOOL CALLING
→ Application defines available tools
→ Direct integration with APIs and services
→ Straightforward for smaller applications
→ Tight control over execution logic
→ Fewer architectural components
→ Works well when integrations are known upfront
🔌 MCP
→ Standardized interface between AI applications and external capabilities
→ Tools and resources can be exposed consistently
→ Useful across multiple AI clients
→ Reduces custom integration patterns
→ Supports increasingly modular agent ecosystems
→ Can improve interoperability between AI systems and tools
But here's where architecture matters.
Imagine your AI agent needs access to:
📧 Email
📁 Documents
🗄️ Databases
🎫 ServiceNow
💬 Slack
☁️ Cloud services
📊 Analytics platforms
🔐 Internal enterprise APIs
Would you build eight custom tool integrations directly into the application?
Or expose capabilities through reusable MCP servers?
🔥 And an even bigger question:
Is MCP replacing APIs and function calling?
I don't think that's the most useful way to look at it.
An MCP tool may still ultimately call an API, database, SDK, or internal service underneath.
The architectural question is really:
Where should the integration contract live?
If you were designing a production Agentic AI platform, what would you choose?
🅰️ Function Calling + APIs
🅱️ MCP-first
🅲️ MCP + APIs + Function Calling together
🅳️ Depends on integration scale and reuse requirements
👨‍💻 AI Engineers & Architects: Are you actually running MCP servers in production?
🎯 Recruiters: How often is MCP appearing in your Agentic AI requirements now?
🤝 Prime Vendors & Implementation Partners: Are clients explicitly requesting MCP experience, or is it still mostly a preferred skill?
🏢 Hiring Managers: Would you rather hire someone who knows MCP—or someone who deeply understands tool architecture, APIs, security and orchestration?
👇 A, B, C or D — and WHY?

The conversation around data analytics in 2026 is fixated on generative AI and faster dashboards. But the trend that is quietly reshaping how we work is the move toward "Data-as-a-Product" thinking, driven by the convergence of Data Mesh principles and the rise of the semantic layer.

Here is the non-obvious reality: the most advanced AI agents and Copilots are only as good as the data products they consume. Without a well-governed, self-serve data mesh, your AI assistant is just generating beautifully formatted hallucinations. The real bottleneck is no longer query speed or compute power; it is data trust and discoverability.

For teams preparing for 2026-2030, the shift is from building pipelines to designing data products. This means treating each domain's dataset as an independent, curated asset with its own SLAs on quality, freshness, and documentation. The most valuable skill is no longer writing the most complex SQL; it is designing the contracts and interfaces that make data reusable without rework.

For my own work, I am moving toward a product-oriented architecture. I focus on defining clear ownership boundaries, implementing automated data quality checks as part of the CI/CD pipeline, and using semantic layers to abstract the complexity of underlying schemas. This reduces the friction between ingestion and insight, allowing the AI layers to work reliably.

Recruiters and hiring managers: I bring deep experience in designing and operationalizing data mesh architectures and semantic layers that turn raw data into trusted, self-serve products. If your team is navigating the shift from project-based analytics to product-based data, I can help build the governance and technical frameworks that make it work.
